interactions.label: Why do most myocardial infarctions arise from atherosclerotic plaques that had n

params.question: Why do most myocardial infarctions arise from atherosclerotic plaques that had not produced critical stenosis?

answers.text: Coronary arteries with mild atherosclerosis lack compensatory remodelling, causing early occlusion

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Early atherosclerotic plaques actually undergo compensatory (outward) remodelling, which is precisely why they can harbour large lipid cores without narrowing the lumen.

answers.text: Thin-cap fibroatheromas have large lipid cores that rupture before producing flow-limiting narrowing

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Thin-cap fibroatheromas have a large necrotic lipid core with minimal fibrous protection. They rupture before producing any flow limitation, exposing the lipid core to blood and triggering thrombosis — the mechanism behind most acute MIs.

answers.text: Non-stenotic plaques generate more turbulent flow, increasing the thrombotic stimulus

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Turbulent flow occurs at stenotic segments, not at mildly diseased ones. It is the morphology of the plaque — thin cap over a large lipid core — that determines rupture risk, not flow dynamics.

answers.text: Calcification in early plaques makes them more brittle and prone to fracture

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Calcification generally stabilises atherosclerotic plaques. Vulnerable plaques are characterised by a thin fibrous cap and large lipid core, not by excessive calcification.

overallFeedback.feedback: The key is plaque morphology, not stenosis severity. Thin-cap fibroatheromas with large lipid cores rupture before causing flow limitation, triggering thrombosis and MI — explaining why most infarctions occur in arteries without prior critical stenosis.

Correct! Vulnerable (thin-cap) fibroatheromas rupture before they narrow the lumen significantly. This explains the clinical paradox of MI without prior angina and why statins reduce cardiac events even without critical stenosis.

interactions.label: A 45-year-old man with Marfan syndrome presents with sudden tearing chest pain r

params.question: A 45-year-old man with Marfan syndrome presents with sudden tearing chest pain radiating to the back. CT angiography reveals a false lumen in the ascending aorta. Which underlying pathology most likely predisposed him to this condition?

answers.text: Atherosclerotic plaque erosion with superimposed thrombus

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Atherosclerotic plaque erosion triggers coronary thrombosis in acute coronary syndromes. Aortic dissection results from a tear in the medial layer, not from intimal plaque events.

answers.text: Cystic medial degeneration with elastic fibre fragmentation

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Cystic medial degeneration — fragmentation and loss of elastic fibres in the aortic media — is the predisposing lesion for aortic dissection. It is accelerated in Marfan syndrome (fibrillin-1 defect), Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, and chronic hypertension. Stanford Type A (ascending aorta) is a surgical emergency.

answers.text: Hyaline arteriosclerosis of the vasa vasorum

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Hyaline arteriosclerosis affects small arterioles in benign hypertension and diabetes, producing homogeneous wall thickening. It does not predispose to aortic dissection.

answers.text: Congenital medial deficiency at an arterial branch point

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Congenital medial deficiency at arterial branch points is the basis of berry aneurysms at the circle of Willis, associated with subarachnoid haemorrhage — not aortic dissection.

overallFeedback.feedback: The answer is cystic medial degeneration. This fragmentation of elastic fibres in the aortic media is the predisposing lesion in aortic dissection, commonly seen in Marfan syndrome, Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, and chronic hypertension.

Correct! Cystic medial degeneration weakens the aortic wall, allowing blood to dissect between the layers. In Marfan syndrome, defective fibrillin-1 accelerates this process. Stanford Type A dissection involving the ascending aorta requires emergency surgery.

interactions.label: A patient diagnosed with STEMI three days ago develops new chest pain and ECG ch

params.question: A patient diagnosed with STEMI three days ago develops new chest pain and ECG changes. Troponin I remains elevated from the initial event. Which biomarker is most useful for confirming reinfarction at this time point?

answers.text: Repeat high-sensitivity troponin I, since any further rise above baseline confirms a new event

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. While troponin is the gold-standard marker for initial MI diagnosis, interpreting a new rise when the initial troponin is still elevated (it remains high for 7–14 days) is unreliable. A marker that has already returned to baseline is more informative.

answers.text: Creatine kinase MB isoform, since it has already normalised and a new peak indicates fresh necrosis

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. CK-MB normalises within 48–72 hours after the initial MI. By day 3, it has returned to baseline — a new peak therefore unambiguously confirms fresh myocardial necrosis, even while troponin remains elevated from the first event.

answers.text: Serum myoglobin, since it rises earliest among all cardiac markers

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Myoglobin rises early but lacks cardiac specificity — it is also elevated in skeletal muscle injury. It cannot reliably distinguish reinfarction from non-cardiac causes of muscle damage.

answers.text: Brain natriuretic peptide, since it increases with new ventricular wall stress

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. BNP reflects ventricular wall stretch and is used to diagnose and monitor heart failure severity, not to confirm acute myocardial necrosis.

overallFeedback.feedback: CK-MB normalises in 48–72 hours, unlike troponin which stays elevated for 7–14 days. By day 3 post-MI, CK-MB has returned to baseline — a second peak confirms new myocardial necrosis even while troponin from the first event persists.
Correct! CK-MB's rapid normalisation (48–72 hours) makes it uniquely valuable for reinfarction detection when troponin remains elevated from the initial event.

interactions.label: During which time window after acute myocardial infarction is the risk of ventri

params.question: During which time window after acute myocardial infarction is the risk of ventricular wall rupture highest?

answers.text: First 6 hours, when coagulative necrosis begins

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. In the first 6 hours, the myocardium appears grossly normal with only wavy fibres microscopically. Coagulative necrosis begins at 12–24 hours, but significant structural weakening has not yet occurred.

answers.text: Days 1–3, during peak neutrophil infiltration

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Days 1–3 bring peak neutrophil infiltration, but the tissue retains enough structural integrity to resist rupture. It is the subsequent macrophage-driven phagocytosis that critically weakens the wall.

answers.text: Days 3–7, when macrophages soften necrotic myocardium

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Between days 3 and 7, macrophages infiltrate and phagocytose necrotic tissue, maximally softening the ventricular wall. This is the peak period for free wall rupture (causing cardiac tamponade), septal rupture (causing VSD), and papillary muscle rupture (causing acute mitral regurgitation).

answers.text: Weeks 2–4, during collagen scar formation

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. By weeks 2–4, granulation tissue and early collagen deposition are actively strengthening the infarct zone, significantly reducing rupture risk.

overallFeedback.feedback: The answer is days 3–7. Macrophages arrive and phagocytose necrotic myocardium during this period, creating maximal wall softening and peak risk for free wall rupture (→ tamponade), septal rupture (→ VSD), and papillary muscle rupture (→ acute mitral regurgitation).
Correct! Days 3–7 are the danger zone — macrophage-mediated softening of necrotic tissue maximally weakens the wall, creating peak risk for free wall, septal, and papillary muscle rupture.

interactions.label: The Frank-Starling mechanism provides sustained compensation in chronic heart fa

params.question: The Frank-Starling mechanism provides sustained compensation in chronic heart failure by indefinitely increasing stroke volume through greater ventricular stretch.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: This statement is false. The Frank-Starling mechanism compensates initially by increasing stroke volume with greater end-diastolic volume. However, chronic overstretching dilates the ventricle past its functional range, ultimately worsening pump failure. Every compensatory mechanism in heart failure eventually 'betrays' the heart.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Correct — this statement is false. While the Frank-Starling mechanism initially boosts stroke volume by increasing ventricular stretch, chronic overstretching dilates the chamber beyond its useful range. All three compensatory mechanisms — Starling, neurohormonal activation, and hypertrophy — ultimately worsen the disease they were meant to correct.

interactions.label: What mechanism produces the nutmeg liver pattern in chronic right heart failure?

params.question: What mechanism produces the nutmeg liver pattern in chronic right heart failure?

answers.text: Portal vein thrombosis causing periportal ischaemic necrosis

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Portal vein thrombosis affects portal inflow, not hepatic venous outflow. The nutmeg pattern specifically results from centrilobular (zone 3) congestion due to raised hepatic venous pressure.

answers.text: Raised venous pressure causing centrilobular congestion in the least oxygenated hepatocytes

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. In right heart failure, elevated central venous pressure distends hepatic sinusoids in zone 3 (centrilobular zone). These hepatocytes are already the least oxygenated — farthest from the portal triad blood supply. The combination of congestion and hypoxia causes centrilobular necrosis, producing the alternating dark and pale zones of the nutmeg pattern.

answers.text: Retrograde bile flow causing diffuse cholestatic injury across all liver zones

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Cholestatic injury causes periportal changes and bile duct proliferation, seen in biliary obstruction — not in congestive hepatopathy from heart failure.

answers.text: Hepatic artery spasm from sympathetic activation causing zone 1 infarction

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Sympathetic activation in heart failure affects systemic haemodynamics but does not produce zone 1 infarction. The nutmeg pattern is driven by passive venous congestion in zone 3, not arterial spasm.

overallFeedback.feedback: The nutmeg pattern results from centrilobular (zone 3) congestion. Raised venous pressure distends sinusoids in the zone where hepatocytes are already least oxygenated, causing necrosis. The alternating dark congested and pale surviving zones produce the classic nutmeg appearance.

Correct! Zone 3 hepatocytes are doubly vulnerable — farthest from the oxygen supply at the portal triad and closest to the congested central veins. Chronic congestion can eventually progress to cardiac cirrhosis.
